Senses.Explanation: Literally ‘a mass of doubt.’ The Chan record makes doubt materially mass-like: a discourse says that inside and outside ‘roll into one mass of doubt’ (滾作一箇疑團), and other records speak of making the whole body, sitting, walking, dressing, eating, and even the encountered world into that mass. The same physical grammar governs its end: it is ‘broken through’ (打破疑團), or remains ‘unbroken’ (疑團不破). In an autobiographical public account, repeated blows make the speaker's mass of doubt more acute (疑團愈切). Thus the phrase is not merely ordinary uncertainty; these later Chan records deploy it as the consolidated, bodily condition named around sustained investigation and its reported breaking. The corpus does not make the mass a separate object from the doubt or state a further gloss for the breaking.
Senses.Note: 301 raw hits in 127 allowlist texts. The strongest deployment is concentrated in Song through Ming/Qing instructional and autobiographical records. No separate ordinary sense was needed: every curated witness names doubt figured as a consolidated mass.

Occurrences.Kwic: 非內、非外，滾作一箇疑團，行不知行、坐不知坐，如一人與萬人敵，又如心心常似過橋時。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Boshan Yuanlai describes inside and outside rolling into one mass of doubt, with walking and sitting no longer distinguished.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: The same discourse uses the recurring physical predicate: break through the mass of doubt.

Occurrences.AttributionNote: Boshan's warning calls the whole body, inside and outside, one mass and pairs it with the fixed unbroken form.

Senses.Explanation: Literally 'the feeling/state of doubt' (疑 doubt + 情 feeling, condition). In these texts it is what the cited texts say arises when a word or saying is raised for investigation (話頭, ‘word or saying’), and the texts describe it in bodily terms — knotted on the brows, impossible to put down. Boshan (Wuyi Yuanlai) defines it outright: 'when exerting effort, what matters is raising the doubt; and what is the doubt?' (做工夫貴在起疑情。何謂疑情？) — 'born, you don't know whence you came, so you cannot but doubt your place of coming; dead, you don't know where you go…'; when the pivot of life and death will not break, 'the doubt suddenly erupts, knotted on your very brows; you can't put it down and can't drive it off' (疑情頓發，結在眉睫上，放亦不下，趂亦不去), until one morning you 'smash the ball of doubt' (撲破疑團). Its measure is the stock line 'great doubt, great awakening; small doubt, small awakening; no doubt, no awakening' (大疑大悟，小疑小悟，不疑不悟). Dahui ties it to life and death: 'if the doubt is not broken, life and death press in' (疑情不破。生死交加). Gaofeng recounts his own case: brooding on 'the myriad things return to one — where does the one return?' (萬法歸一。一歸何處), 'from this the doubt suddenly erupted, so that I could not tell east from west, could not tell south from north' (自此疑情頓發。直得東西不辨。南北不分). The same graded formula reached Xueyan Zuqin as the advice that struck him — 'to investigate Chan you must raise the doubt; small doubt, small awakening' (參禪須是起疑情。小疑小悟) — spoken to him by Librarian Lai of Chuzhou (處州來書記) and preserved in Xueyan's general address (普說). In these texts the doubt is a felt mass — knotted on the brows (結在眉睫上) and held until it bursts (撲破疑團) — not ordinary doubting of this or that. Dahui's record carries the rationale as a saying: 'students today mostly do not doubt themselves — they doubt others; hence the saying: under great doubt there is necessarily great awakening' (今時學道者多不自疑。却疑他人。所以道。大疑之下必有大悟, T47n1998A). The Discourse on Forging in the Chan Gate (禪門鍛鍊說) quotes the graded maxim and sets the word against mere phrase-holding: 'the ancients said: great doubt, great awakening; small doubt, small awakening; no doubt, no awakening. So if the doubt is at ten parts, the awakening is at ten parts. And there are those in the world who teach people to hold the saying dead without raising the doubt — this is the great disease of investigating Chan' (古云：大疑大悟，小疑小悟，不疑不悟。故疑有十分，斯悟有十分。而世有教人死守話頭，不起疑情者，此參禪大病也, X63n1259). Its absence is a live interview topic — Ruo'an asked: 'when the doubt does not arise, what then?' — the master: 'what principle have you seen?' (箬庵問：「疑情不起時如何？」師云：「汝見甚麼道理？」, J25nB171) — and Boshan's letters diagnose it: 'the doubt not arising is the life-and-death mind not being urgent' (疑情不起是生死心不切, the Essential Collected Sayings of Great Master Boshan Wuyi 博山無異大師語錄集要, J27nB197).
Senses.Note: One corpus-wide sense, belonging to the vocabulary of looking at the saying (看話): the word travels with 'raise the doubt' (起疑情) and the word raised (話頭). Strongly multi-source across Linji-line masters — Dahui (the earliest witness here), Gaofeng of his line and Gaofeng's teacher Xueyan — plus the later Caodong master Boshan, who gives the explicit definition. Widely attested (208 allowlist texts). The witnesses from 'Spurring Advance through the Chan Barrier' (禪關策進) are from an anthology, but each section head names a master (verified: 'Chan Master Gaofeng Miao of Tianmu instructs the assembly' 天目高峯妙禪師示眾 = Gaofeng; 'the general address of Chan Master Xueyan Qin of Yuanzhou' 袁州雪巖欽禪師普說 = Xueyan) — though the Xueyan witness's specific line is speech reported inside his general address (普說), the advice of Librarian Lai of Chuzhou (處州來書記), so that occurrence carries a null MasterName. Zen-allowlist grep counts: the doubt (疑情) 936 hits in 208 of 462 texts; 'raise the doubt' (起疑情) 121, 'the doubt suddenly erupts' (疑情頓發) 62, 'the doubt unbroken' (疑情不破) 13, 'the doubt not arising' (疑情不起) 12; the companion 'ball of doubt' (疑團) 288 ('break the ball of doubt' 破疑團 92); the graded maxim's members 'no doubt, no awakening' (不疑不悟) 32, 'small doubt, small awakening' (小疑小悟) 29, and Dahui's 'under great doubt there is necessarily great awakening' (大疑之下必有大悟) 3 (T47n1998A, T47n1999, X70n1392).

Dahui's Recorded Sayings (大慧語錄), in the letter answering Vice-Director Lü Longli (答呂郎中隆禮). Dahui on the doubt (疑情): unbroken, life and death press in; broken ('if the doubt is broken' 疑情若破), the life-and-death mind is cut off.

Occurrences.Kwic: 一歸何處。自此疑情頓發。直得東西

Brooding on the saying 'the myriad things return to one — where does the one return?' (萬法歸一，一歸何處), 'from this the doubt suddenly erupted, so I could not tell east from west.'

Occurrences.Kwic: 參禪須是起疑情。小疑小悟。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Spurring Advance through the Chan Barrier (禪關策進), under 'the general address of Chan Master Xueyan Qin of Yuanzhou' (袁州雪巖欽禪師普說). Xueyan recounts what he did at nineteen: the line 'to investigate Chan you must raise the doubt; small doubt, small awakening; great doubt, great awakening' (參禪須是起疑情。小疑小悟。大疑大悟) is Librarian Lai of Chuzhou's (處州來書記) admonition, which struck Xueyan and made him change the saying he was holding (便改了話頭). This is reported speech inside Xueyan's address, so MasterName is null.

Senses.Explanation: Literally, idle or unnecessary (閑) kudzu-and-wisteria creepers (葛藤). The parent term's Chan use is verbal tangle; this exact compound sharpens it to talk treated as idle or unnecessary. An early record warns people not to gather and talk idle vine-tangle, adding that the old man may catch and examine them. Two later verses call the whole great treasury of teachings 'idle vine-tangle': one immediately adds that the seventeen hundred cases trip people to death. A separate verse says that a massive volume already carries idle vine-tangle and puns that there is no need to send more 'idle furnishings.' The Zen deviation is the extension of the corpus's vine-language from individual words to gathered discussion, large books, the canon, and the case collection. The texts make those appraisals; this entry does not generalize them to every written record.
Senses.Note: Exact-form count: 5 hits in 5 allowlisted texts. The orthographic variant idle vine-tangle (閒葛藤) has 2 hits in 2 texts. One verbal-entanglement sense, cross-checked against vine-tangle (葛藤), spinning out vines (打葛藤), vine-tangle case (葛藤公案), and cutting off the vines (截斷葛藤). The D-canon witness was not curated under the Chinese-Chan-only gate.

Occurrences.Kwic: 莫空不識好惡矻矻地聚頭說閑葛藤。莫教老漢見捉來勘不相當搥折脚。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Direct warning against gathering to talk idle vine-tangle, followed by threat of examination.

Senses.PreferredTarget: an at-ease person of the Way
AlternateTargets: an unoccupied person of the Way
an idle person of the Way
Senses.Explanation: Literally, "an idle or at-ease person of the Way" (閑道人). Chan usage bends ordinary idleness into a named epithet, most often in the full line "an at-ease person of the Way who has ended study and does nothing contrived" (絕學無為閑道人). Huangbo explains that people of old heard one statement and thereby "ended study" (絕學), and so received this name; he contrasts them with people seeking much knowledge and many explanations. Tianru explicitly lists "the great sea of extinction" (大寂滅海), "the ground of actual principle" (實際理地), and this full epithet as different names for "great rest" (大休). The Mirror Record distinguishes accumulating study, ending study, and then passing beyond both, saying that only on reaching the end of study does one first draw near the Way. Other records deploy the shortened term in verse: the whole world is full of people seeking buddha, but an at-ease person of the Way is hard to find (茫茫盡是覓佛漢，舉世難尋閑道人). The epithet therefore names a Chan roster type through explicit ending-study and great-rest definitions, not a generic loafer.
Senses.Note: The exact short form has 37 hits in 33 allowlisted texts. Its stable expansion is 'ended-study, doing-nothing-contrived, at-ease person of the Way.' Evidence includes explicit naming formulas, a list of synonyms, prose distinctions among kinds of study, and verse deployment. The ordinary reading 'idle person' alone misses the corpus-defined epithet.

Occurrences.Kwic: 古人心利纔聞一言便乃絕學所以喚作絕學無為閑道人今時人只欲得多知多觧廣求文義
Occurrences.AttributionNote: The Record of Ancient Venerables preserves Huangbo's naming formula and contrasts the epithet with seeking much knowledge and explanation.

Occurrences.Kwic: 謂之大寂滅海，謂之實際理地，謂之絕學無為閑道人，皆大休之異名也。
Occurrences.AttributionNote: Tianru gives three explicit names for great rest, including the full epithet.

Occurrences.Kwic: 如此一念萬年、萬年一念，猶太虛空，不與萬象森羅為礙，豈不名絕學無為閑道人也。

Occurrences.Kwic: 習學既盡。謂之絕學無為閑道人。及至絕學。方始與道相近。直得過此二學。是謂真過。
